title: Chapter 2.1 — Writing and Graphing Inequalities

explanation: An [[kw:inequality]] is a mathematical sentence that compares two expressions using <, >, ≤, or ≥.
Key phrases: [[imp:'less than']] (<), [[imp:'greater than']] (>), [[imp:'at most'/'no more than']] (≤), [[imp:'at least'/'no less than']] (≥).
To write an inequality from words, identify the two expressions being compared and choose the correct symbol.
The variable can be on either side: $ x < 5 $ is the same as $ 5 > x $.
Pay close attention to whether the boundary value is included (≤, ≥) or not (<, >).

rows.2: at most, no more than, maximum

rows.1: is greater than or equal to
rows.2: at least, no less than, minimum

blocks.title: Writing Inequalities from Phrases

discoveryHook.scenario: A sign says 'You must be at least 48 inches tall to ride.' That single phrase captures a whole range of heights. Inequalities let us describe ranges — everything from speed limits to minimum balances — with just a few symbols.

steps: Identify the expression: 'a number w minus 3.5' = $ w - 3.5 $.
Identify the comparison: 'is less than or equal to' = ≤.
examples.prompt: Write the sentence as an inequality: 'A number w minus 3.5 is less than or equal to −2.'

examples.prompt: Translate 'Three is less than a number n plus 5' into an inequality.
examples.title: B – Reversing the Order
steps: The expression 'a number n plus 5' is $ n + 5 $.
Inequality: $ 3 < n + 5 $, which is equivalent to $ n + 5 > 3 $.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why can this also be written as $ n + 5 > 3 $?

examples.prompt: Write 'Zero is greater than or equal to twice a number x plus 1' as an inequality.
examples.title: C – At Least/At Most

confusionCorner.title: Flipping the Inequality
confusionCorner.body: If you rewrite $ 3 < x $ as $ x > 3 $, the inequality symbol flips. The small end always points to the smaller quantity. [[imp:Don't change the meaning]] when swapping sides.

teacherCues: Write '<, >, ≤, ≥' on the board. Ask students to brainstorm real‑life phrases that mean each symbol.
Display a sentence: 'A number w minus 3.5 is less than or equal to −2.' Ask: 'How would you translate this into symbols?'

discoveryHook.scenario: If a ride requires you to be at least 48 inches tall, 48 inches is okay, 50 inches is okay, but 47 inches isn't. Each of these is a possible solution to the height inequality. Inequalities often have infinitely many solutions — they describe whole intervals, not just one number.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: −2 is not less than −1, so no.

hints: It's the collection of values that make the inequality true.

explanation: A [[kw:solution of an inequality]] is a value that makes the inequality true when substituted for the variable.
An inequality can have many solutions. The set of all solutions is called the [[kw:solution set]].
To check a solution, replace the variable with the given value and simplify. If the resulting statement is true, it's a solution.
Unlike equations, inequalities usually have [[imp:infinitely many solutions]] forming a range of numbers.

formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Substitute and simplify. If true, it's a solution.} $$
notes: Test more than one value to understand the solution set.
Use open/closed circles to mark boundaries.
formulaCard.title: Checking a Solution

teacherCues: Write 'x + 5 ≥ −2' and ask: 'Is −6 a solution? How do you know?'
Emphasize: A solution makes the inequality true, just like an equation.

confusionCorner.title: Negative Values Don't Switch the Sign During Checking
confusionCorner.body: When you substitute a negative number, the inequality symbol stays the same. The direction only reverses when you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, not when you substitute.

confusionCorner.body: Don't confuse the type of circle with the shading direction. An open/closed circle depends on whether the value is included; the shading depends on whether values are larger or smaller.
confusionCorner.title: Circle Direction vs. Shading Direction

examples.title: A – Graphing with a Closed Circle
steps: Draw a number line with -3 marked.
Use a closed circle at -3 because of ≤.
Test a point left of -3 (e.g., -4): $ -4 \le -3 $ true. Test right (e.g., 0): $ 0 \le -3 $ false.

explanation: The [[kw:graph of an inequality]] shows the solution set on a number line.
Use an [[imp:open circle]] (○) for < or > when the number is NOT part of the solution.
Use a [[imp:closed circle]] (●) for ≤ or ≥ when the number IS part of the solution.
Shade the number line in the direction of all possible solutions. Test a point to check which side to shade.

blocks.title: Graphing Inequalities on a Number Line

discoveryHook.scenario: A number line graph of an inequality is like a map showing all the allowed values. An open circle says 'you can't include this point,' while a closed circle says 'this point is welcome!' The shading shows the direction of the endless possibilities.

Amusement park signs show height requirements as a simple line on a height chart. That's a graph of an inequality! Reading the graph tells you exactly what heights are allowed, even if the sign doesn't spell out the inequality.

formulaCard.title: Reading an Inequality Graph
notes: Direction: left = less than, right = greater than.

explanation: Given a graph on a number line, you can write the corresponding inequality.
[[imp:Identify the boundary number]] where the circle is placed.
[[imp:Determine the circle type]]: open → < or >; closed → ≤ or ≥.
[[imp:Note the shading direction]]: left → less than; right → greater than.
Write the inequality with the variable on the left for standard form, but both directions are correct.

blocks.title: Writing Inequalities from Graphs

confusionCorner.title: Variable Placement
confusionCorner.body: An inequality like $ x \ge 1.3 $ can also be written as $ 1.3 \le x $. Both are correct. When the variable is on the left, the symbol points toward it for 'greater than or equal to' when shading right.

discoveryHook.scenario: Need to interpret a sign, check a requirement, or draw a graph? The Understand → Solve → Conclude blueprint keeps you on track. Identify what you're comparing, pick the right symbol, and represent it clearly — just like a professional.

examples.prompt: A state law says a vehicle with 2 axles and its contents can weigh at most 40,000 lb. Write and graph the inequality.
examples.title: A – Maximum Vehicle Weight
steps: Solve: Let w = total weight. $ w \le 40{,}000 $.
Conclude: Graph closed circle at 40,000, shade left. All weights up to 40,000 lb are allowed.

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why is the inequality $ 430 + p \le 600 $, and not $ 430 + p < 600 $?
examples.prompt: A wave pool holds 600 people. Currently 430 are inside. Write an inequality for additional people p that can enter.
steps: Conclude: Graph closed circle at 170 (since $ p \le 170 $), shade left.
examples.title: B – Pool Capacity

examples.prompt: A pool's water temperature must be no less than 76°F. Currently 74°F. Write and graph an inequality for the needed increase t.
examples.title: C – Temperature Requirement
steps: Understand: 'No less than' means ≥. Need $ 74 + t \ge 76 $.
Conclude: Graph closed circle at 2, shade right. Temperature must increase by at least 2°F.

confusionCorner.title: Including vs. Excluding the Boundary
confusionCorner.body: In the pool problem, the capacity is 600. If exactly 600 are inside, no more can enter, so $ 430 + p \le 600 $ is correct. Using < would mean 600 is still allowed, which contradicts the maximum capacity.

explanation: The blueprint for inequalities: [[imp:Understand]] the context: what is being compared? What is the boundary?
[[imp:Solve]]: Write the inequality from words or graph, checking the symbol and direction.
[[imp:Conclude]]: Interpret the result. If graphing, draw the correct circle and shading. If checking, state whether a given value is a solution.
This blueprint works whether you are writing, graphing, or interpreting inequalities.

rows.1: Identify the boundary number and comparison type (less than, greater than, etc.).
Write the inequality with the proper symbol and variable.
Graph on a number line or check a given value.

formulaCard.title: Blueprint Summary
notes: Always check whether the boundary is included (≤, ≥) or not (<, >).
Test a value to confirm your graph.

teacherCues: Display the Understand → Solve → Conclude framework adapted for inequalities: Understand (identify the situation and inequality type), Solve (translate words to inequality or graph to inequality), Conclude (interpret the graph or check a value).
Model the blueprint with a real‑world example: the weight limit on a vehicle axle.
